common.name: Name
common.useSelectionHint: Takes the range currently selected in the sheet
common.pastePlaceholder:
Paste numbers separated by new lines, tabs or ;
e.g. 12.5
13.1
11.8
common.pasteMatrixPlaceholder: Paste a table from Excel (tab-separated columns). The first row may contain headers.

errors.badRange: Range “{{ref}}” is not valid. Use the format Sheet1!B2:B40.
errors.noRange: Enter a data range (or click “Use selection”).
errors.noResults: There are no simulation results. Run the simulation first (Simulation tab → Run).
errors.noAssumptions: The model has no active assumptions. Define at least one assumption.
errors.tooFew: At least {{n}} numeric values are needed ({{got}} found).
errors.badSource: This data source is not available for this tool.

tornado.help1: Tornado analysis moves each assumption, one at a time, from a low percentile to a high one (e.g. P10 and P90) while keeping the others at their base value, and measures how much the forecast changes.
tornado.help2: The spider chart shows how the forecast responds as each assumption moves across several percentiles: steeper lines mean more influential variables.
tornado.interpretation: “{{name}}” is the variable that moves the result the most (≈ {{share}} of the total variation). Bars at the top are the critical variables: estimate them carefully and model them as assumptions.
tornado.noEntries: No assumption changes the result: check that the forecast depends on the assumption cells.
tornado.spiderInterpretation: The steeper the line, the more sensitive the forecast is to that assumption. A flat line means the variable has little influence.
tornado.spiderTruncated: Only the {{n}} most influential variables are charted; the table includes all of them.

errors.percentiles: The low percentile must be lower than the high one.

sensitivity.help1: Uses the results of the last simulation. The rank (Spearman) correlation shows the direction and strength of the relation between each assumption and the forecast.
sensitivity.help2: Contribution to variance estimates what percentage of the forecast's uncertainty is explained by each assumption (normalised squared correlation).
sensitivity.none: No sensitivity data for this forecast.
sensitivity.positive: positive (when the assumption rises, the forecast rises)
sensitivity.negative: negative (when the assumption rises, the forecast falls)
sensitivity.interpretation: “{{name}}” is the most influential assumption on “{{forecast}}”: correlation {{rho}}, {{dir}}, explaining about {{share}} of the variance.
sensitivity.hint: Correlations close to 0 (|ρ| < 0.1) mean little influence; you may fix those variables at their base value to simplify the model.
sensitivity.title: Sensitivity of {{name}}

scenarioTable.help1: Computes the forecast for every combination of two assumptions (like an Excel two-variable data table).
scenarioTable.help2: Useful to see, for example, the NPV for different prices and volumes. Other assumptions stay at their base value.
scenarioTable.needTwo: At least two active assumptions are needed.
scenarioTable.empty: Choose two assumptions and their ranges, then click “Calculate”.
scenarioTable.title: Scenario table of {{name}}
scenarioTable.summary: Base forecast value: {{base}}. In the table it ranges from {{min}} to {{max}}.
scenarioTable.signHint: Red cells are combinations with a negative result (e.g. NPV < 0 ⇒ the project is not worth it); blue cells are positive.

fit.help1: Fits probability distributions to historical data and ranks them by the chosen criterion (AIC, BIC, Kolmogorov–Smirnov or Anderson–Darling).
fit.help2: Select a row to see the histogram with the fitted curve and the P–P and Q–Q plots. Then you can create an assumption with that distribution in the cell selected in the sheet.
fit.ksOk: KS test: {{p}} (≥ 0.05) ⇒ no evidence to reject that the data follow this distribution.
fit.ksBad: KS test: {{p}} (< 0.05) ⇒ the distribution does not describe the data well; try another one or use the data directly (custom distribution).
fit.criteriaHint: AIC and BIC: lower is better (they penalise the number of parameters). For the KS, AD and χ² tests, a high p-value means a good fit.
fit.ppHint: If the points follow the diagonal, the distribution describes the centre of the data well.
fit.qqHint: If the points follow the diagonal, the distribution also describes the tails (extreme values) well.
fit.target: It will be defined in cell {{cell}}.
fit.targetReplace: Cell {{cell}} already has an assumption: its distribution will be replaced.
fit.noTarget: Select a cell in the sheet.

errors.none: No distribution could be fitted to these data.

bootstrap.help1: The bootstrap resamples the data with replacement many times and computes the statistic on each resample. It estimates how precise a mean, percentile or standard deviation is without assuming a distribution.
bootstrap.help2: Useful to know whether the simulation needed more trials: a very wide interval means the statistic is imprecise.
bootstrap.interpretation: With {{c}} confidence, the true {{stat}} lies between {{lo}} and {{hi}}.

hypothesis.help1: Compares the means of two samples (two simulated forecasts or two data ranges) with Welch's t-test, which does not assume equal variances.
hypothesis.help2: Null hypothesis H₀: the means are equal. If the p-value is below the significance level α, H₀ is rejected.
hypothesis.reject: H₀ is rejected: the difference is statistically significant.
hypothesis.noReject: H₀ is not rejected: there is not enough evidence of a difference.

meaningReject.two: {{p}}, below α = {{alpha}} ⇒ the means of “{{a}}” and “{{b}}” differ.
meaningReject.greater: {{p}}, below α = {{alpha}} ⇒ the mean of “{{a}}” is greater than that of “{{b}}”.
meaningReject.less: {{p}}, below α = {{alpha}} ⇒ the mean of “{{a}}” is lower than that of “{{b}}”.

hypothesis.meaningNoReject: {{p}}, not below α = {{alpha}} ⇒ the observed difference between “{{a}}” and “{{b}}” may be due to chance.
hypothesis.ruleOfThumb: Rule of thumb: p-value < 0.05 ⇒ significant difference at 5%. With many simulated trials even tiny differences become significant: also look at the size of the difference.

descriptive.help1: Computes the descriptive statistics of a data set (mean, deviation, skewness, percentiles…) and draws its histogram and cumulative distribution.
descriptive.interpCenter: The data are centred at {{mean}} (mean) / {{median}} (median), with a typical spread of ±{{sd}}.
descriptive.skewRight: It is positively skewed (long tail to high values): the mean exceeds the median.
descriptive.skewLeft: It is negatively skewed (long tail to low values): the mean is below the median.
descriptive.kurtNormal: Its tails are similar to a normal distribution.
descriptive.kurtFat: It has heavy tails (more extreme values than a normal).
descriptive.kurtThin: It has light tails (fewer extreme values than a normal).

overlay.help1: Overlays the simulated distributions of several forecasts to compare them (e.g. the NPV of two alternatives). A curve shifted to the right has larger values; a wider one, more risk.

timeSeries.help1: Forecasts a time series (sales, demand, prices…) with moving averages, exponential smoothing, Holt, Holt–Winters, ARIMA or trend lines. “Automatic” tries several methods and picks the one with the lowest error on the latest data.
timeSeries.help2: The bands show the 80% and 95% prediction intervals: the further ahead, the wider the band. Use the forecast as the expected value and the band to define simulation assumptions.
timeSeries.empty: Enter the series, choose a method and click “Forecast”.
timeSeries.interpretMetrics: RMSE and MAE measure the typical error in the units of the series; MAPE, the average percentage error (below 10% is usually considered very good).
timeSeries.theilGood: Theil's U < 1 ⇒ the model forecasts better than assuming the next value equals the last one.
timeSeries.theilBad: Theil's U ≥ 1 ⇒ the model does not beat the naive forecast (repeat the last value); try another method.
timeSeries.acfHint: Bars outside the dashed lines (±1.96/√n) are significant autocorrelations. Spikes at lags 12, 24… suggest seasonality; a slowly decaying ACF suggests a trend (non-stationary series).
timeSeries.decompHint: Decomposition splits the series into a trend, a seasonal pattern repeating every period and a random residual.
timeSeries.decompNeed: Decomposition needs at least {{n}} data points (two full cycles) and a seasonal period greater than 1.
timeSeries.adfStationary: p-value < 0.05 ⇒ the series is stationary (stable mean and variance).
timeSeries.adfNonStationary: p-value ≥ 0.05 ⇒ the series is not stationary (trend or unit root); ARIMA will need differencing (d ≥ 1).
timeSeries.lbOk: p-value ≥ 0.05 ⇒ residuals behave like white noise: the model captured the structure of the series.
timeSeries.lbBad: p-value < 0.05 ⇒ residuals are still autocorrelated: the model can be improved.
timeSeries.seasonalityHint: A strength close to 1 indicates a strong seasonal pattern with that period.

errors.season: Seasonal methods need at least {{n}} data points (two full cycles).
errors.positive: The multiplicative method requires all data to be positive.

regression.help1: Estimates a linear equation Y = b₀ + b₁·X₁ + … + bₖ·Xₖ by least squares. Enter the dependent variable (Y) and one or more independent variables (X), with headers to name them.
regression.help2: Stepwise regression adds or removes variables according to their p-values, keeping only the significant ones.
regression.empty: Enter Y and the X variables, then click “Estimate”.
regression.dropped: {{n}} rows with missing or non-numeric data were skipped.
regression.interpR2: The model explains {{r2}}% of the variation of Y (R²).
regression.fSig: F test: {{p}} (below 0.05) ⇒ the model as a whole is significant.
regression.fNotSig: F test: {{p}} (not below 0.05) ⇒ the model as a whole is not significant.
regression.interpCoef: For each additional unit of “{{name}}”, “{{y}}” {{dir}} by {{b}} units, all else equal (significant at 5%).
regression.dwOk: Durbin–Watson close to 2 ⇒ no important autocorrelation in the residuals.
regression.dwBad: Durbin–Watson far from 2 (< 1.5 or > 2.5) ⇒ possible residual autocorrelation: p-values may be unreliable.
regression.vifBad: Some variables have VIF > 10 ⇒ multicollinearity: those X are highly correlated with each other and their coefficients are unstable.
regression.pHint: * p-value < 0.05 ⇒ the variable is significant (its coefficient differs from zero). ⚠ VIF > 10 ⇒ multicollinearity.
regression.residualHint: Residuals should look like a patternless cloud around 0. A funnel shape indicates heteroscedasticity; a curve, a missing non-linear relation.

errors.yOneColumn: The dependent variable (Y) must be a single column.
errors.noX: Enter at least one independent variable (X).
errors.tooFew: Too few data: {{n}} observations for {{k}} coefficients.

stochastic.help1: Simulates future paths of a financial variable (price, exchange rate, interest rate…) and shows a fan chart with the percentiles at each time.

helpProc.gbm: Geometric Brownian motion: the price grows at an average rate (drift) with random shocks proportional to the volatility. The classic model for stock prices.
helpProc.meanReversion: Mean reversion (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck): the variable tends to return to a long-run level; suitable for interest rates, commodity prices or costs.
helpProc.jump: Jump diffusion (Merton): like geometric Brownian motion, with occasional sudden jumps (crises, news).

stochastic.annualHint: Per year when Δt is in years
stochastic.speedHint: Higher ⇒ returns to the mean faster
stochastic.estimatedGbm: Estimated: annual drift {{drift}} and volatility {{vol}}. The initial value is the last data point.
stochastic.interpretation: At the end of the horizon ({{horizon}} years) the median is {{median}} and there is a 90% probability that the value lies between {{p5}} and {{p95}}.
stochastic.finalTitle: Distribution at the end of the horizon

errors.noReversion: The series shows no mean reversion (the AR(1) coefficient is not between 0 and 1).
errors.positive: Prices must be positive to estimate geometric Brownian motion.

optimization.help1: Finds the values of the decision variables (yellow cells) that maximize or minimize a forecast while meeting the constraints.
optimization.help2: Static: evaluates the sheet with assumptions at their base value (fast). Stochastic: runs a short simulation for each candidate and optimizes a statistic (e.g. mean NPV or probability of loss).
optimization.help3: First define the decision variables in the Simulation tab → “Define decision”, with their range and type (continuous, integer, binary).
optimization.stochasticHint: Each evaluation runs a full simulation: use few trials (300–1000) and few evaluations (50–200).
optimization.empty: Set up the objective and click “Optimize”.
optimization.feasibleMsg: Solution found: when you {{sense}} “{{name}}” you get {{value}} while meeting all constraints.
optimization.infeasibleMsg: No solution meeting all constraints was found. Review the limits or widen the decision ranges.
optimization.applied: The optimal values were written to the decision cells.
optimization.frontierHint: Each point is the optimum obtained for a different constraint limit: it shows how much objective is gained by relaxing it (e.g. more return in exchange for more risk).

errors.noDecisions: The model has no decision variables. Define them in Simulation → “Define decision”.

messages.budget: The maximum number of evaluations was reached (increase it to search for better solutions).
messages.aborted: Stopped by the user: the best solution found is shown.

project.help1: Builds the project cash flow (revenue, costs, depreciation, taxes, investment, working capital and salvage value) and computes NPV, IRR, MIRR, payback, profitability index and EAA.
project.help2: With financing, it also computes the equity cash flow (loan, interest, tax shield and principal repayment).
project.help3: “Export with formulas” creates a sheet with the live model: then define assumptions (e.g. price or units) and a forecast on the NPV to run a Monte Carlo risk analysis.
project.salvageHint: Sale value of the assets at the end
project.discountHint: Opportunity cost of capital (hurdle rate / WACC)
project.applyGrowth: Fill the years with this growth starting from year 1
project.perYearHint: Type the year-1 value and use the arrow to project it with an annual growth rate.
project.useLoan: The project is partly financed with a loan
project.verdictReject: The project is not worth undertaking (NPV < 0).
project.verdictIndifferent: The project just recovers the investment and the required return (NPV = 0).
project.npvMeaning: NPV = {{npv}}: the additional wealth the project creates after recovering the investment and earning the required rate of {{rate}}.
project.irrMeaning: IRR = {{irr}}: the project's own return. Accept if IRR > {{rate}} (discount rate).
project.multipleIrr: Warning: the cash flow changes sign several times and has more than one IRR ({{irrs}}). The IRR is not reliable then; decide with NPV or MIRR.
project.paybackMeaning: The investment is recovered in {{p}} years (horizon: {{h}} years).
project.noPayback: The investment is not recovered within the horizon.
project.equityMeaning: Equity cash flow: NPV = {{npv}}, IRR = {{irr}}. Compare it with the cost of equity.
project.exportHint: Sheet created. The NPV is in {{npv}}. For risk analysis: define a forecast on {{npv}} and assumptions on the data cells (e.g. price in {{price}} or units in {{units}}).
project.profileHint: NPV falls as the discount rate rises; the IRR is the rate where the curve crosses zero.

npvIrr.help1: Computes NPV, IRR (and every IRR when the flow changes sign several times), MIRR, payback periods, profitability index and EAA of any cash flow.
npvIrr.help2: The first value is period 0 (usually the investment, negative) and is not discounted.
npvIrr.flowsHint: Investments and outflows with negative sign.
npvIrr.empty: Enter the cash flows and click “Calculate”.
npvIrr.noIrr: This cash flow has no IRR (it does not change sign or never crosses zero).

loan.help1: Generates a loan amortization schedule: French (level payment), German (level principal) or American (interest only, principal at the end).
loan.help2: The rate is per period: for monthly payments, use the monthly rate (e.g. 12% nominal annual ⇒ 1% monthly).

explain.french: French method: all payments are equal; early payments are mostly interest and later ones mostly principal.
explain.german: German method: the same amount of principal is repaid each period, so payments decrease.
explain.american: American method: only interest is paid and the whole principal is repaid with the last payment.

depreciation.help1: Compares depreciation methods: straight line, declining balance, double declining balance, sum of years' digits and units of production.
depreciation.help2: Depreciation is not a cash outflow, but it lowers taxes: accelerated methods bring that tax saving forward and increase the NPV.
depreciation.interpretation: Every method depreciates the same total (cost − salvage); only the timing changes. Accelerated methods depreciate more at the beginning.

costOfCapital.help1: Computes the cost of equity with CAPM (including country risk), the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) and converts nominal, effective and real rates.
costOfCapital.help2: WACC is the usual discount rate for the project cash flow; the cost of equity (Ke), for the equity cash flow.
costOfCapital.relever: Compute the levered beta from the industry's unlevered beta (Hamada)
costOfCapital.capmFormula: Ke = Rf + β·(Rm − Rf) + country risk = {{rf}} + {{beta}} × {{prem}} + {{crp}} = {{ke}}
costOfCapital.useCapm: Use the CAPM cost of equity ({{ke}})
costOfCapital.waccMeaning: WACC = {{wacc}}: the minimum return the project must earn to satisfy shareholders and lenders. Use it as the discount rate of the project cash flow.
costOfCapital.fisher: (1 + nominal) = (1 + real)·(1 + inflation). Use the real rate for constant-currency flows and the nominal rate for flows that include inflation.

breakEven.help1: Accounting break-even: the quantity that must be sold to cover all costs (profit = 0).
breakEven.help2: Model break-even: finds the value of an input cell (price, units, cost…) that makes a forecast, such as the NPV, equal to 0. It shows how much that variable can worsen before the project stops being worthwhile.
breakEven.accMeaning: You must sell at least {{units}} units (revenue of {{revenue}}) to avoid losses.
breakEven.safetyGood: Expected sales exceed break-even: they could drop {{s}} before causing losses.
breakEven.safetyBad: Expected sales do not reach break-even: losses are expected.
breakEven.noMargin: The price does not exceed the variable cost: there is no break-even point (each unit sold loses money).
breakEven.modelEmpty: Choose the input cell and the forecast, then click “Calculate”.
breakEven.modelMeaning: When {{cell}} equals {{root}}, “{{f}}” equals {{target}}. The variable can move {{change}} away from its current value before reaching that point.

errors.cell: Enter a single input cell (e.g. Sheet1!C5).
errors.range: The lower bound must be lower than the upper bound.
errors.noRoot: The forecast does not reach {{target}} within the search range; widen the range.

scenarios.help1: Combines scenarios (pessimistic, base, optimistic…) with their probabilities to obtain the expected value, standard deviation and coefficient of variation.
scenarios.help2: It is a simplified risk analysis: Monte Carlo simulation generalises this idea to thousands of scenarios.
scenarios.sumWarning: Probabilities add up to {{sum}}; they will be normalised to 100%.
scenarios.meaning: On average {{e}} is expected, with a spread of ±{{sd}} across scenarios.
scenarios.cvHigh: CV = {{cv}} > 1 ⇒ risk is high relative to the expected value.
scenarios.cvLow: CV = {{cv}} ≤ 1 ⇒ risk is moderate relative to the expected value.
scenarios.mcHint: For a fuller analysis, define assumptions on the key variables and run a Monte Carlo simulation.
